subject: ITCS217
prompt: A new laptop joins the lecture network and gets its address by DHCP. Put the four DHCP messages in the order they are sent, first to last.
stepExplanations: Discover comes first: the client has no address and looks for any DHCP server.
Offer: a server proposes an address to the client.
Request: the client asks to use the offered address.
Ack: the server confirms, and the client can now use the address.
explanation: Slides 39 to 42 show the same exchange in Wireshark: Discover, Offer, Request, then Ack.

subject: ITCS217
prompt: Host A (10.34.10.44) needs to send to host B (10.34.10.80) on the same LAN. A's ARP cache has no entry for B.

answerTier.prompt: Which destination MAC address does A put on the frame that carries its ARP request?
optionExplanations: Correct: the ARP request frame is a broadcast (slides 49, 56).
All zeros is the empty target-MAC field inside the ARP message, not the frame destination.
A cannot address B directly: B's MAC is exactly what A is asking for.
B is on the same LAN, so A resolves B itself; the gateway is only used for other networks.
misconceptions: Confuses the ARP target-MAC field with the frame destination
Assumes the sender already knows the MAC it is asking for
Thinks ARP always goes through the default gateway

reasonTier.prompt: Why is that the right destination?
answers: A does not know B's MAC yet, so every node must hear it
Broadcast frames reach their target faster than unicast
The switch answers ARP requests on behalf of hosts
The target-MAC field is all zeros, so the frame is too
optionExplanations: Correct: only the node that owns 10.34.10.80 replies, and its reply is unicast (slide 50).
Speed is not the reason; reach is.
In the lecture, host B itself sends the ARP reply (slide 57).
The two fields are separate; the zeros only mark the unknown answer.
misconceptions: Believes broadcast is a speed optimisation
Thinks switches resolve ARP
Merges the ARP payload with the Ethernet header

explanation: An ARP request is broadcast because the sender does not yet know the receiver's link-layer address; the reply comes back unicast.

subject: ITCS217
prompt: Alice (network N1) sends data to Bob on a different network, through routers R1 and R2. Alice's ARP cache is empty. Whose MAC address does Alice's first ARP request ask for?
answers: R2, the router on Bob's network
optionExplanations: Correct: Alice frames the data for her default gateway R1, so she resolves R1's MAC (slide 52).
Bob is on another network; Alice never needs his MAC. R2 resolves it at the last hop (slide 54).
R2 is two links away; R1 resolves R2's MAC for the middle hop (slide 53).
Alice already knows Bob's IP address; ARP resolves IP to MAC, not the reverse.
misconceptions: Treats link-layer addresses as end to end
Skips the first hop
Reverses the direction of ARP
explanation: Each sender only resolves the next hop on its own link: Alice resolves R1, R1 resolves R2, and R2 resolves Bob.

subject: ITCS217
prompt: A packet goes from Alice to Bob through R1 and R2, as on slides 52 to 55. Select ALL values that are the same on every link of the path.
optionExplanations: Correct: the IP header keeps Alice's address (NA) end to end.
Correct: the IP header keeps Bob's address (NB) end to end.
Each router builds a new frame with its own interface as the source.
Each frame is addressed to the next hop only (L1, then L3, then LB).
misconceptions: Believes the original sender MAC travels end to end
Believes the frame is addressed to the final host
explanation: IP addresses identify the two end hosts and stay fixed; link-layer addresses identify the two ends of the current link and change at every hop.

subject: ITCS217
prompt: Match each HDLC frame type to its purpose. Each purpose is used once.
pairExplanations: S-frames carry flow and error control, such as RR and REJ.
U-frames are reserved for system and link management.
explanation: The control field tells the receiver which of the three frame types it has received (slide 23).

subject: ITCS217
topic: Problems the data link layer solves
prompt: In a 16-bit frame, only bits 4, 5, 8 and 11 (counting from 1) are corrupted. How should this error be described?
optionExplanations: Correct: burst length runs from the first corrupted bit (4) to the last (11), so 11 − 4 + 1 = 8. This matches slide 8.
Four is the number of flipped bits, not the length of the burst.
Several corrupted bits close together form one burst error, not separate single-bit errors.
The burst stops at the last corrupted bit; bits 12 to 16 are unaffected.
misconceptions: Counts only flipped bits as the burst length
Treats each flipped bit as a separate error
Assumes the whole frame is the burst
explanation: A burst error is measured from the first to the last corrupted bit; bits inside the burst may or may not be flipped.

subject: ITCS217
prompt: A switch receives a frame for a MAC address that is not in its MAC table. A router receives a packet for a network that is not in its routing table and it has no default route. What does each device do, according to slide 47?
answers: Switch: out every other port. Router: drops it
Switch: drops it. Router: drops it
Switch: out every other port. Router: out every interface
Switch: drops it. Router: out every interface
optionExplanations: Correct: the switch floods unknown destinations in its broadcast domain; the router discards packets it cannot route.
A switch does not drop an unknown destination; it floods it.
A router does not flood; that would spread traffic across separate networks.
This swaps the two behaviours.
misconceptions: Thinks switches discard unknown frames
Thinks routers flood like switches
Swaps switch and router behaviour
explanation: Switches work inside one broadcast domain and flood unknown MACs; routers join different networks and drop packets with no route.

subject: ITCS217
topic: Role of the data link layer
prompt: In 2 to 3 sentences, explain why a router removes the incoming frame and builds a new frame, instead of forwarding the original frame unchanged.
modelAnswer: Each link can be a different type, such as Wi-Fi (802.11) on one side and Ethernet (802.3) on the other, so the next link may need a different frame format. Link-layer addresses only name the two ends of the current link, so the router writes new source and destination MAC addresses for the next hop. The IP packet inside stays the same.
checklist: Says links can be of different types or frame formats
Says link-layer addresses are only valid for one link
Says the IP packet inside is kept unchanged
explanation: Self-graded practice; not scored and not counted as coverage evidence.

subject: ITCS217
prompt: Which HDLC mode lets both stations start a transmission as equal peers?
optionExplanations: Correct: in ABM both combined stations can send commands and responses (slide 21).
In NRM the secondary only transmits after the primary polls it.
In ARM the secondary may start a transmission, but the primary still manages the link.
Only ABM treats the two stations as equal peers.
misconceptions: Thinks polling gives both sides equal rights
Confuses "secondary may initiate" with equal peers
Assumes all modes are symmetric
explanation: The modes differ in who may start a transmission: NRM after a poll, ARM the secondary too, ABM both stations as peers.
